name: Databricks, Inc.
origin_detail: Founded 2013 in San Francisco by seven UC Berkeley AMPLab researchers (incl. Ali Ghodsi, Matei Zaharia, Ion Stoica, Reynold Xin, Patrick Wendell, Andy Konwinski, Scott Shenker) who created Apache Spark (open-sourced ~2010, donated to the Apache Software Foundation in 2013); first round led by Andreessen Horowitz
openness_notes: Open core around foundation-governed projects: Spark is an Apache Software Foundation project (Apache-2.0); Delta Lake (Apache-2.0) went to the Linux Foundation in Oct 2019; MLflow and Unity Catalog are open source. The revenue product, the managed Databricks platform and runtime, is proprietary SaaS. Databricks has moved toward more openness over time (all Delta Lake features open-sourced in 2022; Unity Catalog open-sourced 2024).

license_history.note: Spark donated to the ASF the year Databricks was founded
Announced open source at Spark+AI Summit 2019; hosted by the Linux Foundation from Oct 2019; some Delta features remained proprietary in Databricks' platform
Delta Lake 2.0: all features contributed to the Linux Foundation project
Open-sourcing announced 12 Jun 2024 at Data + AI Summit

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Turned an internal proprietary table format into a foundation-hosted open standard to compete with Apache Iceberg/Hudi
Responded to competitor claims that Delta was effectively proprietary
Announced the same week as the Tabular (Apache Iceberg creators) acquisition, amid a format/catalog war with Snowflake

risk_events: Table-format and catalog war with Snowflake and Apache Iceberg; Databricks bought Tabular (Iceberg creators) in Jun 2024 (reported ~$1B)
Very high valuation multiple (~27x run-rate revenue at $190B) and dependence on AI spending
IPO repeatedly deferred; Ghodsi reportedly ruled out a 2026 IPO, 2027 possible
Nov 2026: WSJ reported early talks for a new raise at ~$225B (unconfirmed)
robustness: Core technologies (Spark at the ASF, Delta Lake at the Linux Foundation, MLflow, Unity Catalog) are foundation-hosted or OSI-licensed and widely used by competitors, so they would survive the company. The company itself is the largest private software firm in this group: >$7B revenue run-rate growing >80% (mid-2026), >1,000 customers above $1M run-rate, and very deep private capital.
physical_science_relevance: Spark and Databricks are used for large-scale scientific data processing (genomics, climate, high-energy physics pipelines) and ML on experimental data; MLflow is widely used for experiment tracking in research ML.
openness_effect_assessment: Academic open source (Spark) created a huge user base and talent pipeline that Databricks monetized via a proprietary managed platform. Unlike database vendors that moved to restrictive licences, Databricks repeatedly opened more (Delta 2019/2022, Unity Catalog 2024), using open, foundation-governed standards as a competitive weapon against Snowflake; its valuation rose from $62B (Dec 2024) to $190B (Aug 2026) during this period.
key_takeaway: Databricks is the strongest case for the academic-spin-out, foundation-governed open-core model: the founders gave Spark to the ASF, kept the commercial value in a managed cloud service, and became the most valuable company in this group (~$190B, Aug 2026) without ever relicensing to a restrictive licence. AI demand, not the open-source projects alone, explains the 2025-2026 valuation surge.
